title: Paychecks, Budgets and Credit
bigQuestion: How do you turn a paycheck into a plan that covers what you need, saves for what is coming and keeps borrowing from taking over?

story.title: The Paycheck That Came Up Short
story.kicker: Jalen worked forty hours at fifteen dollars an hour and had already spent six hundred dollars in his head.
paragraphs: Jalen got his first real job the week after he turned seventeen, stocking shelves and running a register at a grocery store on the North Side. Fifteen dollars an hour, twenty hours a week during the school year. He did the math on the bus home from the interview: twenty hours times fifteen dollars was three hundred dollars a week, so two weeks was six hundred dollars. He had the six hundred spent before he had worked a single shift. A pair of shoes, a phone case, gas money for his cousin, and the rest in a shoebox for a used car.

Two weeks later the pay stub showed up in his email. He scrolled past the top line, where it did say $600.00, and stopped at the bottom, where it said something else. Net pay: $517.38. He read it three times. Then he read the middle, the part he had skipped. Federal income tax. Social Security. Medicare. Illinois income tax. Four lines, each one a small number, all of them adding up to eighty-two dollars and change that he had never seen and never would.

His aunt, who had done payroll for a dental office for twenty years, laughed when he showed her. Not at him. At the memory of her own first check. "Everybody does this," she said. "Everybody spends the gross. You only ever get the net." She pointed at each line and told him where the money went. Then she said the thing that changed how he thought about the job. "The number at the top is what you earned. The number at the bottom is what you have. Build everything on the bottom number."

That night Jalen redid the math. Five hundred seventeen dollars, not six hundred. The shoes could wait. The shoebox got forty dollars instead of a hundred. And he wrote, on an index card he kept in his wallet for the next two years, a single line: plan on the net. This chapter is the long version of his aunt's advice. It covers what leaves a paycheck before it reaches you, how to build a budget on what is left, and how credit works so that you use it instead of the other way around.
story.think: Jalen spent his gross pay in his head before he saw his net pay. Why is that such a common mistake, and what one habit would keep you from making it?

lessons.title: Gross Pay and Net Pay
lessons.mainIdea: Gross pay is what you earned; net pay is what reaches your account after withholding, and every plan has to start from net.
reading: Pick up a pay stub, on paper or on the payroll app, and find two numbers first. The top number is *gross pay*: hours worked times the hourly rate, before anything is taken out. If you worked 40 hours at $15.00 an hour (example), gross pay is $600.00. The bottom number is *net pay*, also called take-home pay. It is gross pay minus every deduction. In Jalen's case it was $517.38. The gap between the two, $82.62 in this example, is *withholding*: money the employer sends to the government on your behalf before you ever touch it.

Between those two numbers the stub lists each deduction on its own line. The usual four for a first job are federal income tax, state income tax, Social Security and Medicare. Some jobs add more: health insurance premiums, a retirement plan contribution, union dues. Each line shows the amount for this pay period and, in another column, the amount so far this year. That second column is labeled YTD, for year to date.

The common mistake is the one Jalen made: budgeting on gross. People hear "fifteen an hour" and multiply, then wonder why the money is short every month. A second mistake is assuming the withholding is a fee you lost. It is not. The income tax lines are a prepayment on the tax you will owe for the year; if too much was withheld, you get the difference back as a refund when you file. The Social Security and Medicare lines fund benefits you will draw on later. The rule: read the stub all the way down, and write your budget from the bottom line, not the top.

words.d: total earnings for a pay period before any deductions; hours times rate for an hourly job
gross pay minus all deductions; the amount actually paid to you, also called take-home pay
money an employer takes out of a paycheck and sends to the government for taxes on the worker's behalf
the running total of pay or a deduction from January 1 through the current pay period, shown as YTD on a stub

look.title: One Pay Stub, Line by Line (example)
look.cite: example stub; withholding amounts vary with your W-4 and pay
look.prompt: Add the four deduction lines. Does gross minus that total equal the net shown? What share of gross pay was withheld?

check.q: A stub shows gross pay of $480.00 and total deductions of $61.50. What is the net pay?
check.why: Net pay is gross pay minus deductions: $480.00 minus $61.50 equals $418.50.

check.q: Which number should a monthly budget be built on?
choices: Gross pay, because it is what you earned
Net pay, because it is what actually reaches you
The hourly rate times 40
The YTD column
check.why: Only net pay is available to spend or save; budgeting on gross leaves you short by the amount withheld.

check.q: What does the YTD column on a pay stub show?
choices: The amount owed next period
The employer's cost for your benefits
The running total since January 1
The number of hours left in the year
check.why: YTD means year to date, the total of that line from the start of the calendar year through this pay period.

lessons.title: Where the Withholding Goes
lessons.mainIdea: Federal and state income tax are prepayments on a yearly bill, while Social Security and Medicare withholding, together called FICA, are fixed shares of every paycheck.
reading: Look at the four deduction lines again, because they are not all the same kind of thing. Two of them, federal income tax and state income tax, are estimates. Income tax is figured once a year on your total income, and the government does not want to wait a year to collect it. So your employer withholds a slice of each check as a prepayment. How big a slice depends on the form you filled out when you were hired, the *W-4*. It tells the employer about your situation so the withholding comes close to what you will owe. Illinois has a flat state income tax, so the state line is a single fixed percentage of your pay.

The other two lines are different. Social Security and Medicare are federal programs that pay retirement, disability and survivor benefits and hospital insurance for older adults. They are funded by a payroll tax called *FICA*, for the Federal Insurance Contributions Act. FICA is not an estimate. It is a set share of your wages: 6.2 percent for Social Security and 1.45 percent for Medicare, 7.65 percent together, taken from every paycheck. Your employer pays a matching amount on top of your wages that never shows on your stub. In the example above, 6.2 percent of $600 is $37.20 and 1.45 percent is $8.70, which is exactly what the stub shows.

Each January your employer sends you a *W-2*, a form that totals your wages and every withholding line for the year. You use it to file a tax return. Filing is where the estimate gets corrected. If the year's withholding was more than the tax you owe, which is common for a student working part time, the difference comes back as a *refund*. If it was less, you pay the rest. A first-job worker who earned a few thousand dollars often owes little or no federal income tax and gets most of that line back, but only by filing. FICA does not come back; it is the price of the coverage it funds.

words.d: the form a new employee fills out so the employer knows how much federal income tax to withhold
the payroll tax that funds Social Security and Medicare; 6.2 percent plus 1.45 percent of wages, matched by the employer
the yearly form from an employer that totals your wages and withholding, used to file a tax return
money returned after filing a tax return because more was withheld during the year than was owed

look.title: Two Stubs, One Question
look.text: Priya and Marcus both earn $600 gross this period at the same store. Priya's stub shows $37.20 for Social Security and $8.70 for Medicare. Marcus's stub shows the same two numbers. But Priya's federal income tax line is $36.72 and Marcus's is $12.10, and Marcus says the store must have made a mistake on Priya's check.
look.prompt: Explain why the FICA lines match to the penny while the federal income tax lines differ, and what form each of them filled out that made the difference.

check.q: Which two deductions together make up FICA?
choices: Federal and state income tax
Health insurance and retirement
Union dues and parking
Social Security and Medicare
check.why: FICA is the payroll tax for Social Security (6.2 percent) and Medicare (1.45 percent), 7.65 percent of wages together.

check.q: What is the Social Security withholding on $400 of gross pay?
check.why: Social Security is 6.2 percent of wages: 0.062 times $400 equals $24.80.

check.q: Why might a part-time student get a refund after filing a tax return?
choices: FICA is returned to students
More income tax was withheld during the year than was actually owed
The employer overpaid the W-2
Refunds are automatic for anyone under 18
check.why: Withholding is an estimate; when it exceeds the year's actual income tax, filing returns the difference. FICA is never refunded.

lessons.title: Checking the Stub for Errors
lessons.mainIdea: Payroll makes mistakes, so check hours, rate and deductions against your own records every pay period and raise a problem the same week.
reading: Payroll is run by software and by people, and both make mistakes. The most common are missing hours, a wrong rate after a raise, overtime paid at straight time, and a deduction that should have stopped. None of them will fix themselves. So build a two-minute habit. When each stub arrives, hold it next to your own record of the hours you worked. Keep that record yourself, in a notes app or a small notebook: the date, clock-in, clock-out, and the total for each shift. Do not rely on memory or on the store's system alone.

Check three things in order. First, hours. Add your shifts for the pay period and compare to the hours line. Second, the rate. Multiply hours by your rate and compare to gross. If you worked more than 40 hours in a week, the extra hours are *overtime* and are paid at one and a half times your regular rate under federal law for most hourly workers. Forty-four hours at $15.00 is not $660.00; it is 40 times $15.00 plus 4 times $22.50, or $690.00 (example). Third, the deductions. The FICA lines should always be 6.2 and 1.45 percent of gross. If they are not, something is wrong.

When you find a problem, act that week. Go to the person who runs payroll, or your manager, with the stub and your record, and ask calmly for the correction. Most errors are honest and get fixed on the next check. Keep every stub, on paper or as a saved file, for the whole year. They are your proof if a W-2 is wrong, and they are the record a landlord or a lender will ask for when you rent an apartment or apply for a loan. *Direct deposit*, where pay goes straight to your bank account, is safer than a paper check and lets you see the money the same day, but it does not replace reading the stub.

words.d: hours over 40 in a workweek, paid at one and a half times the regular rate for most hourly workers under federal law
pay sent electronically straight into your bank account instead of as a paper check
the span of days one paycheck covers, commonly one week, two weeks or half a month

look.title: Find the Error
look.text: Your notebook shows five shifts this two-week period: 8, 8, 6, 8 and 8 hours in week one (38 hours) and 8, 8, 8, 8 and 10 hours in week two (42 hours). Your rate is $15.00. The stub shows 80 hours and gross pay of $1,200.00.
look.prompt: What should the hours line and the gross pay be, counting overtime in week two? What will you bring to payroll to show it?

check.q: A worker earning $15.00 an hour works 42 hours in one week. What is the correct gross pay?
check.why: 40 hours at $15.00 is $600.00, plus 2 overtime hours at $22.50 (one and a half times) is $45.00, for $645.00.

check.q: What is the best record to check a pay stub against?
choices: The store's schedule from the start of the month
A coworker's stub
Your memory of the busy days
Your own written log of each shift's hours
check.why: Your own log of clock-in and clock-out times is the record you control and can show payroll when the numbers disagree.

check.q: Why keep every pay stub for the whole year?
choices: To check the W-2 and to prove income to a landlord or lender
Stubs expire after 30 days
The IRS asks for them with every return
To calculate FICA yourself each week
check.why: Stubs are your proof of wages and withholding if the W-2 is wrong, and the income record landlords and lenders ask for.

lessons.title: Start From Take-Home Pay
lessons.mainIdea: A budget is a monthly plan that assigns every dollar of net pay to a category before the month starts, so spending follows a decision instead of a mood.
reading: Sit down with a blank page, a pencil and your last two pay stubs. A *budget* is nothing more than a plan for money before it arrives. It has three parts: income, expenses and what is left over. Start with income, and use net pay only. If you are paid every two weeks, most months have two checks, so two times net is a safe monthly figure. Jalen's net was $517 every two weeks, so his monthly income line was $1,034 (example). Two months a year have three checks; treat that third check as a bonus, not as income you can count on.

Next, list every expense you know is coming, and sort them into *fixed expenses* and *variable expenses*. Fixed ones are the same every month and usually have a due date: rent, a phone bill, a bus pass, a car payment, insurance. Variable ones change with your choices: groceries, gas, eating out, clothes, entertainment. For fixed, copy the exact amount. For variable, look at the last month's bank statement or receipts and write an honest average. Underestimating groceries is the classic mistake; the budget looks balanced on paper and breaks in the third week.

Now subtract total expenses from income. If the answer is positive, that surplus is what you can save. If it is negative, the budget is not balanced and something has to change: a variable expense comes down, or income goes up. Do not leave a negative number sitting there. The last step is the one people skip: after the month ends, compare what you planned to what you spent, line by line. A budget that is never checked against reality is a wish list. A budget checked every month gets more accurate every month.

words.d: a written plan for a set period, usually a month, that assigns income to expenses and savings before the money is spent
a cost that is the same amount every month, like rent, a phone plan or a car payment
a cost that changes from month to month with your choices, like groceries, gas or eating out
the amount left when expenses are less than income; the money available to save

look.title: Jalen's First Monthly Budget (example)
look.cite: example budget for a part-time worker living at home
look.prompt: Add the six expense and savings lines. How much is left unassigned? Where would you put it, and why?

check.q: Which of these is a fixed expense?
choices: Eating out
A monthly phone plan
Groceries
Movie tickets
check.why: A phone plan is the same amount on the same date every month; the others change with your choices.

check.q: Net pay is $517 every two weeks. What is a safe monthly income figure for a budget?
check.why: Most months contain two paychecks, so two times $517 is $1,034; the occasional third check is a bonus, not planned income.

check.q: Planned expenses total $1,100 and net income is $1,034. What must happen?
choices: Nothing; the gap is small
Add the gap to next month's income
Count the third-check months to cover it
Reduce a variable expense or raise income until the budget balances
check.why: A negative balance means the plan overspends; a budget must be brought to zero or a surplus by cutting variable costs or earning more.

lessons.title: Needs, Wants and Savings
lessons.mainIdea: Sorting every expense into needs, wants and savings, with 50/30/20 as one starting split, shows where a budget can bend and where it cannot.
reading: Take your expense list and put a letter next to each line: N for a *need*, W for a *want*, S for savings. A need is something you cannot go without for long: shelter, food, a way to get to work, a phone if the job requires it, insurance, medicine. A want is everything that makes life better but that you could pause: streaming, takeout, a newer phone, concert tickets. The line between them is not always sharp. Groceries are a need; a $7 coffee on the way to school is a want inside the food category. Be honest, not harsh.

One widely used starting split is the *50/30/20 rule*: about 50 percent of net pay to needs, about 30 percent to wants, and about 20 percent to savings and paying down debt. On $1,034 a month (example), that is roughly $517 for needs, $310 for wants and $207 for savings. It is a guide, not a law. A student living at home with few needs can save far more than 20 percent. An adult paying Chicago rent may find needs eat 60 percent or more, and wants have to shrink to make room. The point of the split is to check the shape of a budget, not to force every budget into one shape.

The order matters more than the percentages. Needs come first and are paid on their due dates. Savings comes second, and the best way to make it happen is to pay it like a bill: move the amount to a savings account on payday, before wants get a turn. Wants get whatever is left, and they are the only category with room to bend. When money is tight, that is the category you cut, and it is also the category people are most tempted to protect. Writing the letter next to each line makes the choice visible before the month starts.

words.d: an expense you cannot safely go without: housing, food, transportation to work, insurance, medicine
an expense that improves life but could be paused without harm, like entertainment or eating out
one starting guide for a budget: about half of net pay to needs, 30 percent to wants and 20 percent to savings and debt

look.title: Sort the List
look.text: Dani's monthly list: rent share $450; groceries $220; CTA pass $75; phone $50; streaming services $35; takeout $120; gym $30; renters insurance $15; savings $100; clothes $60. Her net pay is $1,300 a month (example).
look.prompt: Mark each line N, W or S, total each group, and compare the shares to 50/30/20. Which single line would you change first if her hours got cut?

check.q: Under 50/30/20, about how much of $1,500 net pay would go to savings?
check.why: Twenty percent of $1,500 is $300; the rule puts about 20 percent toward savings and debt payments.

check.q: Which item is a want rather than a need?
choices: Bus pass to get to work
A streaming subscription
Asthma medicine
Groceries
check.why: A subscription can be paused without harm; transportation to work, medicine and groceries are needs.

check.q: What is the most reliable way to make sure savings actually happens each month?
choices: Save whatever is left at the end of the month
Save only in three-paycheck months
Move the savings amount to a separate account on payday, like a bill
Keep the savings in your wallet
check.why: Paying savings first, automatically on payday, keeps wants from spending it; end-of-month leftovers are usually gone.

lessons.title: The Emergency Fund
lessons.mainIdea: An emergency fund is cash set aside for surprises, built to a starter goal first and then toward a few months of expenses, and kept where it is easy to reach but not easy to spend.
reading: A car will not start on a Tuesday. A phone screen cracks. Hours get cut for two weeks. A tooth needs fixing. None of these is a planned expense, and every one of them will happen to you at some point. Without money set aside, a surprise turns into debt: a credit card balance, a loan from a friend, a late rent payment with a fee. An *emergency fund* is cash saved for exactly these moments, so that a bad week does not become a bad year.

Build it in two stages. The first goal is small and fast: a starter fund of a few hundred dollars, enough to cover a tire, a copay or a phone repair. Many people aim for $500 or $1,000 as that first line. At $50 a paycheck it takes twenty checks to reach $1,000 (example), less than a year. Once the starter fund is in place, the longer goal is three to six months of essential expenses, the needs column of your budget. If needs total $900 a month, three months is $2,700. That number can look impossible from a first job. It is not meant to be reached quickly. It is reached by the same $50 a check, over years, while the fund also gets used and refilled.

Where you keep it matters. The fund needs to be *liquid*, meaning you can get to it in a day or two without penalty, so a savings account is the right place, ideally at a bank or credit union separate from your everyday checking. It should not be in cash at home, where it is unsafe and too easy to dip into. It should not be invested in anything that can lose value the week you need it. And it is not the vacation fund or the car fund. Give it its own account with its own name, and when you use it, the next budget line is to refill it.

words.d: savings set aside only for unplanned, necessary expenses such as a car repair, a medical bill or lost hours
able to be turned into cash quickly and without loss; a savings account is liquid, a car is not
a member-owned, not-for-profit financial institution that offers accounts and loans like a bank

look.title: Reaching a Starter Fund (example)
look.cite: example figures; paychecks every two weeks
look.prompt: At $50 a check, how many months does the starter fund take? How many years to reach three months of needs at the same pace?

check.q: Which expense is an emergency fund for?
choices: Concert tickets that sell out fast
A planned spring break trip
A birthday gift
A car repair that must be done to get to work
check.why: The fund covers unplanned, necessary costs; trips, gifts and tickets are planned wants that belong in the regular budget.

check.q: Saving $50 from each of 26 paychecks a year, how much is set aside in one year?
check.why: 26 paychecks times $50 equals $1,300.

check.q: Where should an emergency fund be kept?
choices: In cash in a drawer at home
In a separate savings account you can reach in a day or two
In stocks so it grows faster
In your everyday checking account with spending money
check.why: The fund must be liquid and safe from both loss and casual spending; a separate savings account meets all three.

lessons.title: Debit Against Credit
lessons.mainIdea: A debit card spends money you already have; a credit card borrows money you must pay back, and the two cards behave differently when things go wrong.
reading: Two cards can look identical in a wallet and do opposite things. A *debit card* is tied to your checking account. Tap it at the register and the money leaves your account that day. If the account has $40 and you try to spend $50, the purchase is declined or, if you agreed to overdraft coverage, it goes through and the bank charges an *overdraft* fee, often around $30 or more. Turn overdraft coverage off. A declined card is a small embarrassment; a fee on a $10 sandwich is a real loss.

A *credit card* is a loan. Tap it and the card company pays the store; you now owe the card company. Once a month you get a statement listing what you charged, the total balance, the minimum payment, and the due date. Pay the full balance by the due date and you pay no interest at all. That is the way to use a credit card: as a convenient way to pay for things you already budgeted for, cleared in full every month. Pay less than the full balance and *interest* starts on what is left, and that is where trouble begins.

There are two more differences worth knowing. First, fraud protection. If a stolen debit card drains your checking account, the money is gone from your account until the bank investigates, and rent may bounce in the meantime. If a stolen credit card is used, the charges are on the card company's money while they investigate, and federal law caps your liability at a small amount if you report it promptly. Second, only the credit card builds a credit history, because only it involves borrowing and repaying. A debit card does nothing for your score no matter how carefully you use it. The rule: debit for everyday spending if you are still learning, credit only when you can pay it in full every month.

words.d: a card linked to a checking account that spends your own money immediately
a card that borrows from the card issuer for each purchase; the balance must be repaid, with interest on any part not paid by the due date
spending more than a checking account holds; the bank may cover it and charge a fee
the cost of borrowing money, charged as a percentage of the amount owed

look.title: Two Wallets, One Stolen Phone
look.text: Sam and Lee both have their phones stolen with their cards saved in the wallet app. Sam's is a debit card; the thief spends $400 from Sam's checking account before Sam notices, and Sam's rent payment is due in two days. Lee's is a credit card; the thief charges $400 to it. Both report the theft the same evening.
look.prompt: Whose money is actually missing tonight, whose rent is at risk, and why does the same theft land so differently on the two of them?

check.q: What happens when you pay a credit card's full statement balance by the due date?
choices: Interest is charged on half the balance
The minimum payment is added to next month
No interest is charged on those purchases
The card is closed until next statement
check.why: Paying the full balance on time means nothing is borrowed past the due date, so no interest is charged.

check.q: Why is turning off overdraft coverage on a debit card a good idea for a new account holder?
choices: It raises the credit score
It makes the card work overseas
It doubles the daily limit
A declined purchase costs nothing, while an overdraft usually costs a fee of about $30
check.why: Overdraft coverage lets a purchase go through and then charges a fee; a decline simply stops the purchase.

check.q: Which card use builds a credit history?
choices: A credit card paid in full each month
A debit card used daily
A prepaid gift card
Cash withdrawals from an ATM
check.why: Only borrowing and repaying is reported to credit bureaus; debit and prepaid cards involve no borrowing.

lessons.title: APR and the Minimum Payment
lessons.mainIdea: APR is the yearly cost of a balance, charged month by month, and paying only the minimum keeps most of the balance and its interest alive for years.
reading: Open a credit card statement and find the *APR*, the annual percentage rate. It is the yearly interest rate on any balance you carry past the due date. Card APRs commonly run in the twenties or higher. To see what it costs each month, divide by twelve. A 24 percent APR (example) is about 2 percent a month. Carry a $1,000 balance and the interest for one month is about $20. That $20 is added to the balance, so next month you owe $1,020 before you buy anything else.

Now find the *minimum payment*, the smallest amount the card company will accept without calling you late. It is usually a small percentage of the balance or a flat floor like $25, whichever is larger. Here is the trap. On that $1,000 balance at 2 percent a month, a $25 minimum pays $20 of interest and only $5 of the actual debt. The balance drops to $995. At that pace the card is paid off in years, not months, and the total interest paid can be several times the price of whatever was bought. The card company designs the minimum this way. It is legal, it is printed on the statement, and it is the single most expensive habit a young adult can pick up.

The fix is arithmetic, not willpower. Pay the full balance every month if you can. If you cannot, pay as far above the minimum as the budget allows, and stop adding new charges until the balance is gone. Every statement now carries a required box that shows how long the balance will take to pay off at the minimum and what it would cost; read it. A *late fee* and a possible APR increase follow any payment that misses the due date, so set the payment to go automatically a few days early. And before choosing a card, compare APRs and annual fees on the printed terms, not the rewards on the ad.

words.d: annual percentage rate; the yearly interest rate charged on a balance, divided by 12 for the monthly rate
the smallest amount a card issuer accepts each month; paying only this keeps most of the balance and its interest going
the total amount currently owed on a credit account
a charge added when a payment arrives after the due date; often followed by a higher APR

look.title: One Month on a $1,000 Balance at 24% APR (example)
rows: part of payment that reduces the debt, $
look.cite: example; 24% APR divided by 12 gives 2% per month
look.prompt: If the cardholder paid $120 instead of $25, what would the balance be after this month? Roughly how many months would it take to clear at $120?

check.q: A card has an 18 percent APR. What is the monthly interest rate?
choices: 18 percent
1.5 percent
0.18 percent
6 percent
check.why: Monthly rate is APR divided by 12: 18 divided by 12 is 1.5 percent.

check.q: On a $1,000 balance at 2 percent per month, a $25 payment is made. How much of it reduces the debt?
check.why: Interest for the month is $20; only the $5 above the interest reduces the balance.

check.q: What is the surest way to avoid credit card interest entirely?
choices: Pay the minimum on time every month
Use the card only for large purchases
Choose a card with rewards
Pay the full statement balance by the due date every month
check.why: Interest is charged only on a balance carried past the due date; paying in full means there is none.

lessons.title: Compound Interest, Both Directions
lessons.mainIdea: Compound interest pays interest on interest, which makes savings grow faster over time and makes unpaid debt grow the same way against you.
reading: Put $1,000 in an account that pays 10 percent a year (an example rate, chosen for easy arithmetic). After one year you have $1,100. The second year the 10 percent is figured on $1,100, not $1,000, so you earn $110 and have $1,210. The third year you earn $121 and have $1,331. Each year's interest is bigger than the last because it is earned on the interest that came before. That is *compound interest*. Simple interest would have paid $100 flat each year, for $1,300 after three years. The gap is small at first and enormous over decades, which is why the most powerful ingredient in saving is not the amount but the number of years.

A quick tool for seeing this is the *Rule of 72*: divide 72 by the yearly rate to estimate how many years money takes to double. At 6 percent, 72 divided by 6 is 12, so money doubles about every 12 years. At 3 percent it takes about 24 years. Start at 18 and a single doubling, then another, then another, happens before retirement. Start at 40 and there is time for far fewer. This is also why a savings account, which today pays a low rate, and a retirement account, which can hold investments that have historically grown faster over long periods, do different jobs.

Now run it in reverse. An unpaid credit card balance compounds exactly the same way, at a much higher rate, and the growth is against you. A $1,000 balance at 24 percent APR with no payments at all would grow by about $20 the first month, then about $20.40 the second, then more, and would roughly double in about three years by the Rule of 72. That is the same force that builds savings, pointed the other way. The rule that follows: compound interest should be working for you in a savings account and never against you on a card. Every dollar of high-interest debt paid off is a guaranteed return at that card's APR, which no savings account can match.

words.d: interest figured on the original amount plus all the interest already added, so growth speeds up over time
interest figured only on the original amount, the same flat sum each period
an estimate: 72 divided by the yearly rate gives the years for money to double at compound interest
the original amount saved or borrowed, before any interest is added

look.title: $1,000 at 10% a Year, Compounded (example)
look.cite: example with a round rate; each year's interest is 10% of the previous total
look.prompt: By how much does compounding beat simple interest after four years? Use the Rule of 72 to estimate when the $1,000 becomes $2,000.

check.q: $1,000 earns 10 percent compound interest per year. What is the balance after two years?
check.why: Year one: $1,100. Year two: 10 percent of $1,100 is $110, giving $1,210. Simple interest would give only $1,200.

check.q: Using the Rule of 72, about how long does money take to double at 8 percent a year?
choices: 8 years
9 years
18 years
72 years
check.why: 72 divided by 8 is 9, so about nine years.

check.q: Why is paying off a 24 percent APR card balance called a guaranteed return?
choices: The card company pays a bonus for early payoff
Paid-off debt is added to your savings account
Every dollar paid stops 24 percent compound interest from growing against you, which no savings account matches
Interest is refunded when the balance reaches zero
check.why: Removing debt that compounds at 24 percent saves exactly that rate; it is the same force as compound savings, pointed the right way.

lessons.title: Credit Scores in Plain Terms
lessons.mainIdea: A credit score is a number built from your borrowing record, driven mostly by paying on time and keeping balances low, and it sets the price and the possibility of future borrowing and renting.
reading: When you apply for a car loan, an apartment, or sometimes a job, someone pulls your *credit report*. It is a record kept by three companies, the credit bureaus, of every loan and credit card you have had: when it opened, the limit, the balance, and whether each payment was on time. A *credit score* is a single number squeezed out of that report. The most common scoring model runs from 300 to 850. Higher is better. Roughly, scores in the high 600s and up are treated as good by most lenders, and scores in the mid 700s and above get the best terms. A person with no credit history has no score at all, which is its own problem: lenders cannot tell whether you are reliable.

Two things drive most of the score. The biggest is *payment history*: whether every payment arrived on time. One payment more than 30 days late can stay on the report for years and knock the score down hard. The second is how much of your available credit you are using, called *utilization*. A card with a $1,000 limit carrying a $900 balance looks risky; the same card at $100 looks careful. Keeping balances well under a third of the limit helps. Smaller factors are how long your accounts have been open, how many new accounts you have applied for recently, and the mix of account types.

Building a score from nothing takes patience, not tricks. One starter card, or being added as an authorized user on a trusted family member's long-standing card, used for a small regular charge and paid in full and on time every month, builds a record over a year or two. Do not apply for several cards at once; each application is a hard inquiry that dents the score briefly. Check your own report free at least once a year through the official site, AnnualCreditReport.com, and dispute any account you do not recognize. A good score means a lower APR on a car loan, a landlord who says yes, and a lower deposit on utilities. A poor one makes every one of those cost more, which is why the habit that builds it is the same one from the last lesson: pay on time, in full.

words.d: the record kept by credit bureaus of your loans and cards, their balances and whether payments were on time
a number, commonly on a 300 to 850 scale, that summarizes how reliably you have borrowed and repaid
the record of whether each payment was made on time; the largest factor in a credit score
the share of your available credit you are using; a balance near the limit lowers a score
a lender's check of your report when you apply for credit; several in a short time lower a score slightly

look.title: Two Applicants, One Apartment
look.text: A landlord pulls two reports. Applicant A has one credit card open for two years, a $1,500 limit, a current balance of $120, and 24 on-time payments. Applicant B has three cards opened in the last four months, limits totaling $3,000, balances totaling $2,700, and one payment 45 days late last month. Both earn the same income.
look.prompt: Name the factors that separate the two scores, say which applicant the landlord will likely choose, and list the first two things Applicant B should change.

check.q: What is the single largest factor in a credit score?
choices: Your income
Your age
The number of cards you own
Whether payments have been made on time
check.why: Payment history carries the most weight; income is not part of a credit score at all.

check.q: A card has a $1,000 limit. Which balance is best for the utilization part of a score?
check.why: Low utilization, well under a third of the limit, signals careful use; balances near the limit lower the score.

check.q: Where can you check your own credit report for free without harming your score?
choices: Only through a paid monitoring app
AnnualCreditReport.com, the official free site
By applying for a new card and reading the decision
Reports cannot be viewed by the consumer
check.why: Federal law gives you free access to your reports through AnnualCreditReport.com; checking your own report is not a hard inquiry.

review.q: Gross pay is $720 and net pay is $612. What is the total withholding?
review.why: Withholding is gross minus net: $720 minus $612 is $108.

review.q: Which deduction is a fixed percentage of every paycheck rather than an estimate corrected at tax time?
choices: Federal income tax
FICA (Social Security and Medicare)
State income tax refund
Health insurance premium
review.why: FICA is 6.2 percent plus 1.45 percent of wages on every check; income tax withholding is an estimate settled when you file.

review.q: A worker at $16.00 an hour works 44 hours in a week. What is correct gross pay?
review.why: 40 hours at $16.00 is $640.00, plus 4 overtime hours at $24.00 is $96.00, for $736.00.

review.q: A monthly budget lists $1,200 income and $1,250 of expenses. What is the right first move?
choices: Put the $50 on a credit card
Skip savings this month and next
Count on a third paycheck
Cut a want until expenses are at or below $1,200
review.why: A budget must balance; wants are the category built to bend, and debt or skipped savings only move the gap forward.

review.q: Which of these is the emergency fund meant to cover?
choices: A sudden car repair needed to get to work
A new video game on release day
Holiday gifts
A planned weekend trip
review.why: The fund is for unplanned, necessary costs; planned wants belong in the regular budget.

review.q: A $1,000 card balance at 24 percent APR gets a $25 payment. About how much of the balance is actually paid down?
review.why: Monthly interest at 2 percent is $20, so only $5 of the $25 reduces the balance.

review.q: $2,000 earns 10 percent compound interest per year. What is the balance after two years?
review.why: Year one: $2,200. Year two: 10 percent of $2,200 is $220, giving $2,420.

review.q: Which habit does the most to build a strong credit score?
choices: Opening several cards in one month
Keeping balances near the limit to show use
Using a debit card for everything
Paying every bill on time and keeping card balances low
review.why: Payment history and low utilization are the two biggest factors; debit use is not reported and many new applications hurt.
